subject: Medicine
summary: Gallstones are solid deposits that form in the gallbladder, often causing biliary colic or complications like cholecystitis. Diagnosis relies on imaging and clinical pattern, while management ranges from observation to surgery.

sections.p: Gallstones are crystalline concretions of cholesterol, bilirubin, or mixed composition that develop in the gallbladder. Diagnosis requires typical pain plus imaging showing stones or sludge.
b: Ultrasound is first‑line: stones appear echogenic with posterior shadowing.
CT or MRCP if ultrasound is equivocal or complications suspected.

t.b: Does the patient have stones or sludge? Positive: echogenic focus with shadowing confirms gallstones.

t.a: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin)
t.b: Is there biliary obstruction? Elevated ALP and bilirubin suggest obstruction; normal values do not rule out stones.

sections.p: Severity is judged by presence of complications: uncomplicated biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, gallstone pancreatitis, or gallstone ileus.
b: Mild: episodic colic, no inflammation.
Moderate: acute cholecystitis or choledocholithiasis.
Severe: pancreatitis, perforation, or gallstone ileus.

sections.p: Stone formation follows the “four F’s”: Fat, Female, Fertile, and Forty, plus additional risk factors common in low‑resource settings.
b: Obesity and high‑cholesterol diet → cholesterol stones.
Pregnancy, estrogen therapy → supersaturation of cholesterol.
Hemolytic diseases (sickle cell, malaria) → pigment stones.
Chronic infections (TB, HIV, schistosomiasis) → biliary stasis and pigment stones.

sections.p: Typical biliary colic is a sudden, severe right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder, lasting 30‑60 minutes, often after a fatty meal.
b: Pain may be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sweating.
Fever, jaundice, or a rigid abdomen suggest complications.

sections.p: Imaging and labs guide diagnosis and urgency. When a test is unavailable, clinical judgment and bedside ultrasound (if possible) are essential.
b: Ultrasound for stones and gallbladder wall thickness.
MRCP for ductal stones when ultrasound is inconclusive.

t.b: Is there a common bile duct stone? Positive: filling defect in duct confirms choledocholithiasis.
Is pancreatitis present? Elevated >3× normal supports gallstone pancreatitis.

sections.p: Complications can become life‑threatening and require urgent care.
b: Fever, leukocytosis, RUQ tenderness → acute cholecystitis.
Jaundice with right upper quadrant pain → choledocholithiasis.
Severe epigastric pain, high lipase → gallstone pancreatitis.
Abdominal distension, vomiting → gallstone ileus.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve obstruction, and prevent recurrence. Surgical removal is definitive; medical therapy is supportive.
b: Analgesia (NSAIDs) for pain; avoid opioids that delay gallbladder emptying.
IV fluids and antibiotics for acute cholecystitis (cover Gram‑negatives and anaerobes).
Ursodeoxycholic acid for small cholesterol stones when surgery is not possible.
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is first‑line for symptomatic stones; open surgery if severe inflammation.
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) to clear common duct stones before surgery.

sections.p: After treatment, counsel on lifestyle and monitor for recurrence or complications.
b: Weight loss, low‑fat diet, regular exercise reduce cholesterol stone risk.
Screen for hemolysis in patients with recurrent pigment stones.
Post‑cholecystectomy ultrasound if persistent symptoms.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic gallstone pain or imaging findings.
b: Peptic ulcer disease – epigastric pain unrelated to meals.
Biliary dyskinesia – functional pain without stones.
Acute hepatitis – RUQ pain with markedly raised transaminases.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring or alarming.
b: Normal LFTs do not exclude choledocholithiasis; imaging is required.
Ultrasound may miss small (<3 mm) duct stones; consider MRCP if suspicion remains.

faq.q: Why are cholesterol stones more common in women?
faq.a: Estrogen increases cholesterol secretion into bile, making it more lithogenic.

faq.q: Can gallstones be treated without surgery?
faq.a: Small cholesterol stones may dissolve with ursodeoxycholic acid, but surgery is preferred for symptomatic disease.
A palpable, non‑tender gallbladder with jaundice suggests malignant obstruction, not gallstones.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology behind cholesterol versus pigment gallstones.
Describe the diagnostic work‑up for a patient with suspected acute cholecystitis.
Outline the management steps for gallstone pancreatitis.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect a focused history and perform a systematic abdominal exam to identify biliary colic, inflammation or obstruction.
b: Ask about onset, character, radiation (right shoulder), duration, relation to meals, nausea/vomiting, fever, jaundice, weight change, pregnancy, estrogen use, hemolysis, TB/HIV history
Check for risk factors: obesity, high‑fat diet, rapid weight loss, chronic liver disease, malnutrition
Examine for right upper quadrant tenderness, Murphy’s sign, rebound, guarding, costovertebral angle tenderness
Assess for jaundice, scleral icterus, skin pallor, bruising, ascites, abdominal distension
Check vitals: pulse, BP, temperature, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation
Review medications and herbal supplements

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a tiered approach: bedside ultrasound first, then labs and advanced imaging if needed.

t.b: Detects gallstones, gallbladder wall thickness (>3mm), pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy’s sign. Positive if echogenic foci with shadowing and wall thickening.

t.a: Liver function tests (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, bilirubin)
t.b: Elevated ALP/GGT and conjugated bilirubin suggest obstructive jaundice; transaminases rise in acute cholecystitis.
Lipase >3× upper limit indicates pancreatitis; amylase is less specific.
Leukocytosis (>10,000/µL) supports infection; anemia may indicate hemolysis.
Shows common bile duct stones, strictures, or biliary anatomy when ultrasound equivocal.
Identifies gallstone ileus, perforation, or alternative pathology.
Assesses gallbladder ejection fraction; poor function (<35%) supports chronic cholecystitis.
Separates conjugated vs unconjugated; conjugated rise indicates obstruction.
Use clinical criteria: RUQ pain >2 hrs, nausea, vomiting, fever, and Murphy’s sign to diagnose acute cholecystitis.

sections.p: Classify based on complications and organ involvement.
b: Uncomplicated biliary colic – episodic RUQ pain, no inflammation or obstruction
Acute cholecystitis – RUQ pain, fever, leukocytosis, Murphy’s sign, gallbladder wall thickening
Choledocholithiasis – RUQ pain, jaundice, dilated CBD (>6mm) on imaging
Gallstone pancreatitis – epigastric pain, lipase >3× ULN, imaging evidence of CBD stone
Gallstone ileus – small bowel obstruction with ectopic stone on imaging
Severe complications – perforation, sepsis, multi‑organ failure

sections.p: Differentiate gallstone disease from other causes of RUQ pain and jaundice.

t.b: Pain starts periumbilical, migrates to RLQ; Murphy’s sign negative; ultrasound shows inflamed appendix.
Epigastric pain improves with food; no RUQ tenderness; normal LFTs.
Persistent pain, weight loss, abnormal LFTs, imaging shows mass.
Jaundice, ascites, peripheral edema; cardiac auscultation abnormal.
Diffuse right upper quadrant tenderness, elevated transaminases, no gallstones on ultrasound.
Weight loss, epigastric pain, normal LFTs, CT shows mass.

sections.p: A structured approach ensures safe care from initial assessment through definitive therapy and follow‑up, with clear triggers for escalation or referral in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Stabilise: assess airway, breathing, circulation; give IV crystalloid if dehydrated; treat severe pain with IV opioid titration; give anti‑emetic if vomiting.
2. Diagnose urgency: bedside RUQ ultrasound; if unavailable, use focused clinical criteria (RUQ pain >6 h, fever, leukocytosis) to presume acute cholecystitis.
3. Start empiric antibiotics for suspected infection: broad‑spectrum covering Gram‑negatives and anaerobes (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole). Avoid fluoroquinolones in pregnancy.
4. Provide biliary drainage when obstruction or sepsis present: urgent percutaneous cholecystostomy if surgery not feasible; endoscopic sphincterotomy if choledocholithiasis and endoscopy available.
5. Definitive treatment: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy for uncomplicated acute cholecystitis within 72 h; open surgery if severe inflammation or limited laparoscopy resources.
6. Post‑operative monitoring: vitals, urine output, wound assessment, serum bilirubin and amylase on day 1; discharge when afebrile, tolerating diet, pain controlled with oral analgesics.
7. Escalate or refer: persistent fever >48 h, rising bilirubin, signs of perforation, or failed drainage → higher‑level centre or surgical team.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Antibiotics and analgesics are the main pharmacologic tools; awareness of adverse effects prevents iatrogenic harm.
b: Ceftriaxone: may cause biliary sludge and pseudolithiasis; monitor liver function and discontinue if jaundice worsens.
Metronidazole: neurotoxicity with prolonged use; stop if peripheral neuropathy develops.
Fluoroquinolones: tendinopathy and QT prolongation; avoid in patients with cardiac arrhythmia or pregnancy.
Opioids (e.g., morphine, fentanyl): risk of sphincter of Oddi spasm worsening pain; use lowest effective dose and consider non‑opioid analgesics.
NSAIDs: can precipitate renal impairment in dehydration; give only if renal function acceptable and avoid in active peptic ulcer disease.
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA): used for small cholesterol stones; may cause diarrhoea; stop if diarrhoea severe.

sections.p: Recognise early signs of deterioration; timely escalation reduces mortality in gallstone disease.
b: Acute cholecystitis progressing to gangrene or perforation: increasing abdominal rigidity, tachycardia, hypotension → urgent surgical review.
Choledocholithiasis with rising bilirubin >250 µmol/L or worsening cholestasis: arrange ERCP or refer for urgent biliary drainage.
Gallstone pancreatitis with serum lipase >3 × upper limit and persistent pain >48 h: admit to high‑dependency unit, monitor for necrosis, consider early ERCP if biliary obstruction persists.
Gallstone ileus: obstruction signs, air‑fluid levels, Rigler’s triad on imaging → immediate laparotomy with enterolithotomy.
Sepsis (temperature >38 °C, WBC >12 ×10⁹/L, lactate >2 mmol/L): start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and transfer to ICU if organ dysfunction.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions modify presentation, laboratory interpretation and therapeutic choices in gallstone disease.
b: HIV/TB: higher incidence of pigment stones; antiretroviral drugs may cause cholestasis; avoid hepatotoxic antibiotics when liver enzymes >3 × ULN.

Pregnancy: gallbladder stasis increases stone risk; use ultrasound only, avoid CT; treat acute cholecystitis with IV antibiotics safe in pregnancy (e.g., cefazolin) and defer surgery until second trimester if possible.
Malnutrition: low gallbladder motility, predisposes to stones; correct protein‑calorie deficit before elective surgery.
Diabetes: autonomic neuropathy blunts pain, may mask perforation; tighter glucose control peri‑operatively, monitor for infection.
Alcohol excess: can cause pancreatitis; differentiate gallstone‑related from alcohol‑related by imaging and lipase trends.
Renal failure: limit nephrotoxic NSAIDs; adjust antibiotic dosing; avoid contrast‑enhanced CT if GFR <30 mL/min.
Liver failure: coagulopathy increases bleeding risk; correct INR with vitamin K or plasma before surgery.
Age extremes: infants rarely develop stones; elderly have higher peri‑operative risk, favour early drainage over delayed surgery.

sections.p: Tailored strategies address the unique needs of children, pregnant women, the elderly, HIV‑positive patients and facilities with limited resources.
b: Children: cholesterol stones uncommon; focus on hemolytic causes; use MRCP if ultrasound inconclusive; laparoscopic cholecystectomy preferred when indicated.
Pregnancy: prioritize maternal safety; use ultrasound for diagnosis; give cefazolin for infection; perform laparoscopic cholecystectomy in second trimester if urgent.
Elderly: higher comorbidity; consider percutaneous cholecystostomy as bridge to surgery; monitor for delirium and cardiac events.
HIV‑positive: screen for opportunistic biliary infections; choose antibiotics without significant CYP450 interactions with antiretrovirals; consider prophylactic antifungals if CD4 <200 cells/µL.

Low‑resource settings: rely on bedside RUQ ultrasound; if unavailable, use clinical scoring (pain >6 h, fever, leukocytosis) to start antibiotics and arrange transfer for drainage; use oral UDCA for small cholesterol stones when surgery not feasible.

facts: Four F’s risk: Fat, Female, Fertile, Forty; add obesity, high‑cholesterol diet, estrogen, hemolysis, chronic infection
Ultrasound sensitivity >90% for stones >3 mm; posterior acoustic shadow confirms
Choledocholithiasis defined by CBD diameter >6 mm (or >8 mm if post‑cholecystectomy) on US
Acute cholecystitis diagnosis requires two of: RUQ pain, fever >38°C, leukocytosis >12 ×10⁹/L, US wall thickening >3 mm
Gallstone pancreatitis severity: serum lipase >3× ULN and CT evidence of necrosis; severe if organ failure >48 h
Murphy’s sign: inspiratory arrest on deep RUQ palpation indicates gallbladder inflammation
ERCP indicated for cholangitis (Charcot’s triad) or persistent biliary obstruction after 48 h
Gallstone ileus classic Rigler’s triad: pneumobilia, ectopic gallstone, small‑bowel obstruction on plain X‑ray

vivas.q: Define a cholesterol stone versus a pigment stone
vivas.a: Cholesterol stones are radiolucent, >70% cholesterol, linked to supersaturation; pigment stones are black or brown, contain calcium bilirubinate, associated with hemolysis or infection

vivas.q: What is the bedside test for acute cholecystitis and how is it performed?
vivas.a: Positive Murphy’s sign: ask patient to inhale deeply while you press under the right costal margin; pain with inspiratory arrest indicates inflammation

vivas.q: Interpret a CBD diameter of 9 mm on ultrasound in a post‑cholecystectomy patient
vivas.a: Suggests choledocholithiasis; further imaging (MRCP) or ERCP is warranted

vivas.q: Why is routine pre‑operative antibiotics given before cholecystectomy?
vivas.a: To reduce postoperative wound infection and intra‑abdominal sepsis, especially in acute cholecystitis

vivas.q: How do you differentiate gallstone ileus from simple small‑bowel obstruction clinically?
vivas.a: History of intermittent biliary colic, pneumobilia on imaging, and elderly female predisposition point to gallstone ileus

vivas.q: A patient with known gallstones presents with small‑bowel obstruction; imaging shows an impacted stone near the terminal ileum. What is the specific term?
A 30‑year‑old female with RUQ pain and gallstones reports pain radiating to her right shoulder. This shoulder pain is an example of:
vivas.a: Kehr’s sign, referred pain via phrenic nerve irritation

vivas.q: During elective cholecystectomy, which structure forms the medial boundary of Calot’s triangle?
vivas.a: The cystic duct forms the medial border

vivas.q: A stable, afebrile patient with chronic symptomatic gallstones – what is the appropriate management principle?
vivas.a: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is indicated; no emergency surgery needed

vivas.q: Which benign lesion most commonly causes luminal biliary obstruction?
During laparotomy for incarcerated hernia, what specific action addresses an incidental gallstone in the peritoneum?
vivas.a: Enterotomy and stone extraction (enterolithotomy) followed by fistula closure if present

vivas.q: Immediate surgical procedure for gallstone ileus to relieve obstruction?
vivas.a: Enterolithotomy – removal of the obstructing stone via enterotomy

vivas.q: Best imaging modality for a young woman with lower abdominal pain to assess gallstones, cholecystitis, ectopic pregnancy, or pelvic pathology?
vivas.a: Transabdominal pelvic ultrasound, which can visualize gallbladder and pelvis

vivas.q: What are the key history questions for suspected biliary colic?
vivas.a: Onset, duration, radiation, relation to meals, relieving factors, associated nausea/vomiting, fever, jaundice, past stones, pregnancy, hemolysis

vivas.q: Explain why ERCP is avoided in uncomplicated biliary colic.
vivas.a: ERCP carries risk of pancreatitis; without ductal obstruction it offers no benefit

vivas.q: How does HIV infection alter gallstone disease presentation?
vivas.a: Higher incidence of pigment stones, atypical presentations, and increased risk of cholangitis due to opportunistic infections

vivas.q: What bedside test cannot reliably differentiate between cholesterol and pigment stones?
vivas.a: Physical examination; stone composition requires analysis of expelled stones or imaging characteristics

vivas.q: When ultrasound is unavailable, what bedside tool can aid diagnosis of gallstone disease?
vivas.a: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) probe can detect gallbladder stones and wall thickening

mcqs.q: A 55‑year‑old woman presents with RUQ pain, fever 38.5°C, WBC 14 ×10⁹/L, and US shows gallbladder wall 4 mm. What is the next best step?
mcqs.e: Acute cholecystitis requires antibiotics first; surgery after stabilisation

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for cholesterol gallstones?
mcqs.e: Sickle cell disease predisposes to pigment stones

mcqs.q: A patient with gallstone pancreatitis has persistent jaundice after 72 h. Which investigation is most appropriate?
mcqs.e: MRCP best visualises ductal stones non‑invasively

mcqs.q: Which sign on plain abdominal X‑ray suggests gallstone ileus?
mcqs.e: Rigler’s triad (pneumobilia, ectopic stone, obstruction) is classic

mcqs.q: In a pregnant woman with symptomatic gallstones, the safest initial imaging is:
mcqs.e: Ultrasound avoids radiation and is first‑line in pregnancy

mcqs.q: Which medication is contraindicated in acute biliary colic?
mcqs.e: Anticholinergics may worsen sphincter spasm and are not indicated

cases.v: 45‑year‑old female, BMI 32, presents with 4‑hour RUQ pain radiating to right shoulder after a fatty meal, nausea, no fever. US shows 8‑mm stone in GB, wall 2 mm, CBD 5 mm.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

qs.a: IV fluids, NSAID analgesia, observation; schedule elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy

qs.q: Which bedside sign would you look for to rule out acute cholecystitis?
qs.a: Negative Murphy’s sign (no pain on inspiratory arrest)

cases.v: 70‑year‑old male, known gallstones, presents with vomiting, abdominal distension, X‑ray shows air in biliary tree and a calcified oval density in right iliac fossa. No fever.

qs.q: What condition does this picture represent?

qs.a: Enterolithotomy to extract the stone and relieve obstruction

qs.q: Is fistula repair required at the same operation?
qs.a: Usually deferred; address later if symptoms persist

mistakes: Listing cholesterol and pigment stones without mentioning mixed stones
Confusing Murphy’s sign (inspiratory arrest) with McBurney’s point tenderness
Prescribing antibiotics for uncomplicated biliary colic
Recommending CT as first‑line imaging for gallstones
Omitting the need for ERCP in cholangitis with jaundice
Failing to consider pregnancy when ordering radiographs
